questions.q: Which of these random variables is **continuous**?
options: The number of heads in 10 coin flips
The number of emails received in an hour
The face shown by a die
A person's exact height in cm
questions.explain: Continuous variables are measured and can take any value in a range (170.539… cm). The others are counted, so they are discrete — you cannot get 2.5 heads.

questions.q: For a continuous height variable, what is $P(\text{height} = 170.0000\ldots \text{ cm exactly})$?
options: The height of the density curve at 170
$0$ — only ranges (areas under the curve) have positive probability
It depends on the bucket width
questions.explain: A single exact point has zero width, so zero area. Continuous probability is the area under the density over an interval; the density value itself is not a probability.

questions.q: Flipping 10 fair coins, the random variable $X$ = number of heads. What is $P(X = 5)$?
questions.explain: $P(X = 5) = \binom{10}{5} / 2^{10} = 252/1024 \approx 0.246$. 5 is the most likely count but far from certain; $0.1$ wrongly assumes the 11 counts are equally likely.

questions.q: In the "bridge" lab, what happens as the height buckets shrink from 10 cm toward 0.1 cm (with enough people)?
options: The bars all become equally tall
The density histogram approaches a smooth density curve — which is why sums ($\sum$) become integrals ($\int$)
The total area under the bars grows without bound
questions.explain: Shrinking the measuring stick turns the discrete histogram into a continuous density. The total area stays 1, and summing over buckets becomes integrating over the curve.
